screens.title: System Auditing and Logging
screens.narratorSegment: System logs are the primary evidence of what happened on a Linux server. They record user logins, service starts and stops, kernel messages, and application output. In practice, logs power troubleshooting, performance investigations, and security detection. If you can read, filter, and rotate logs reliably, you can find the root cause of many incidents and preserve evidence when something goes wrong. In this chapter we focus on two complementary stacks: traditional syslog daemons such as rsyslog for collecting and forwarding text logs, and the systemd journal managed by journald for structured, queryable logs. We also cover tools you will use every day: journalctl for targeted queries and logrotate to keep files from growing indefinitely. You will learn concrete configuration examples, how to make the journal persistent across reboots, and how to write a logrotate policy for a custom application. By the end you will be able to inspect service logs, centralize logs if needed, rotate and compress old files, and run basic analyses to find failed logins or repeated errors. Consider which log file on your system you would protect first and why.

screens.title: System Logs: What and Why
screens.narratorSegment: System logs are chronological records of events produced by the kernel, init systems, services and applications. They capture state changes such as user authentication events, service start and stop events, kernel warnings, and application errors. Logs are essential because they provide an audit trail for troubleshooting and security investigations. For example, when a service crashes, log entries around the crash time reveal the preceding actions and error messages. A concrete scenario: a sudden spike in failed SSH authentication entries in auth. log indicates either a misconfiguration or a brute force attempt. Without logs you cannot determine the origin or timeline. A common misconception is that logging is passive and low priority; in reality, logs must be intentionally configured, rotated, and protected. If logs are world-readable or not rotated, you risk exposure or disk exhaustion. Key operational concerns include choosing which events to log, ensuring timestamps are consistent, and securing log files with correct permissions. As a takeaway, treat logs as critical telemetry: decide what to preserve, where to store it, and how long to keep it so you can answer who did what and when.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.4 › System Logs: What and Why
Definition

What are system logs?

Chronological records produced by kernel, system services, and applications that document events, errors, and activity.

Sources
Kernel messages, systemd/journal, daemons like sshd, application stdout/stderr, and cron jobs.
Operational role
Troubleshooting, incident response, compliance, and capacity planning.
Common misconception
Assuming default logging is always sufficient. Many systems require tailored logging levels and retention policies.
Concrete Example
Failed SSH attempt analysis

Look in auth.log for repeated "Failed password" lines, extract IP addresses, and count occurrences to find persistent attackers.

sudo grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $11}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr
Key Takeaway

Treat logs as primary evidence. Decide what to collect, ensure retention, and secure access to those files.

screens.title: rsyslog Basics: Facility and Priority
screens.narratorSegment: rsyslog is a traditional syslog daemon used widely to collect and forward text-based system messages. Two core concepts drive rsyslog rules: facility and priority. A facility indicates the source or category of a message — examples include auth, mail, cron, and kernel. Priority indicates severity levels like info, warning, error, crit and emerg. In configuration files you combine facility and priority to decide where messages go. For instance, the rule authpriv.* /var/log/auth. log records all authentication-related messages in a dedicated file. Another common rule, *. info;mail. none;authpriv. none;cron. none /var/log/messages, writes all informational messages except those from mail, authpriv, and cron to a general file. Practically, group sensitive logs like authentication into separate files so access controls can be stricter. A frequent mistake is mis-ordering rules or forgetting to escape characters; always validate syntax and restart the rsyslog service after changes. As a takeaway, use facility and priority intentionally to separate sensitive messages and simplify later analysis. rsyslog Basics: Facility and Priority means use facility and priority selectors to direct messages to the right files and destinations for clarity and security.. In practical terms, how rsyslog classifies and routes messages. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.4 › rsyslog Basics
Core Concept

Facility and Priority

Facilities identify the origin of messages. Priorities express severity. Combine both to route logs.

Example rules
authpriv.*                   /var/log/auth.log
*.info;mail.none;authpriv.none;cron.none    /var/log/messages
First line sends authentication messages to auth.log. Second line sends most info-level messages to messages while excluding mail, authpriv, and cron.
Operational tip
After editing /etc/rsyslog.conf or files under /etc/rsyslog.d/, restart rsyslog with systemctl restart rsyslog to apply changes.
Concrete Scenario
Separate auth logs for security

Storing auth events in /var/log/auth.log lets you limit access and quickly scan failed authentication attempts without noise from other services.

Common mistake

Applying broad selectors without exclusions can flood general logs and bury sensitive entries. Use explicit exclusions when needed.

Key Takeaway

Design selectors so sensitive content is separated and general messages remain readable for daily monitoring.

screens.title: Configuring rsyslog for Centralization
screens.narratorSegment: Centralizing logs to a dedicated collector simplifies monitoring and preserves logs if an individual host is compromised. To configure a collector, enable the appropriate input modules in rsyslog. For UDP, uncomment module(load="imudp") and enable input(type="imudp" port="514"). For TCP you can enable imtcp similarly. On clients, add a forwarding rule such as *.* @logserver_ip:514 to send messages via UDP or *.* @@logserver_ip:514 for TCP. Always secure the transport where possible, for example by using TLS or a private network. After editing configuration files on both sides, restart rsyslog on collector and clients. A common operational step is to apply filters on the collector to place incoming messages into host-specific directories or to tag them for easier indexing. Misconfiguration risks include port conflicts, firewall blocking, or unintentional flooding of the network with logs. As a practical check, generate a test message with logger and confirm it appears on the collector. This ensures forwarding and reception are working end-to-end. Configuring rsyslog for Centralization means forward logs to a dedicated, secured collector to simplify analysis and protect evidence from compromised hosts.. In practical terms, enable receiving on a collector and forward from clients. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.4 › Configuring rsyslog for Centralization
Collector Setup

Enable inputs and listen on the network so one server can receive logs from many clients.

module(load="imudp") input(type="imudp" port="514") # or for TCP # module(load="imtcp") # input(type="imtcp" port="514")
Restart with systemctl restart rsyslog and ensure firewall allows the chosen port.
Client Forwarding

Add a forwarding rule on clients to send all or filtered messages to the collector.

*.* @logserver_ip:514        # UDP forward
*.* @@logserver_ip:514       # TCP forward
Test

Use the logger command to generate a message on the client and confirm it appears on the collector.

screens.title: journald and journalctl
screens.narratorSegment: systemd's journald collects logs from multiple sources — the kernel, initrd, services and applications that write to standard output or standard error. Unlike plain text files, journald stores logs in a structured binary journal which enables powerful querying. journalctl is the command-line tool that reads this journal and provides rich filters. Unlike tailing text files, you can filter by unit name, priority, process ID, time range, and output format such as JSON for programmatic parsing. A common confusion is to think journald replaces rsyslog; they serve complementary roles. You can forward journal entries to a syslog daemon or have rsyslog collect text files, so use both where appropriate. Another important operational note: by default journald stores logs in volatile memory under /run/log/journal, which is lost on reboot. If you need persistent logs, create /var/log/journal and restart systemd-journald. In short, journald offers fast, structured querying while rsyslog excels at stable, text-based forwarding and long-term storage. journald and journalctl means use journalctl for fast, precise queries and make journald persistent when you need durable logs across reboots.. In practical terms, how systemd's journal stores and exposes logs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.4 › journald and journalctl
What journald does

Structured collection

Journald collects and stores log records in a binary format with fields for unit, PID, priority and more.

# Show all journal entries journalctl # Follow new entries in real time journalctl -f
Key differences
  • journald stores structured binary entries; system logs are plain text files managed by rsyslog.
  • journalctl offers filters by unit, priority, PID and time ranges for precise querying.
  • Use rsyslog to forward or archive logs to long-term storage; use journald for quick, local analysis.
Key Takeaway

Leverage journald for fast filtering and rsyslog for long-term archival and centralization when needed.

screens.title: Essential journalctl Queries
screens.narratorSegment: journalctl offers concise filters that save time when you search for evidence. Start with the basics: journalctl shows the full journal while journalctl -f follows new entries in real time. To view logs for a single service, use journalctl -u followed by the unit name; for example, filtering sshd quickly surfaces authentication-related messages from that daemon. To inspect kernel messages only, use journalctl -k. You can limit results by time range with --since and --until for targeted investigations. Priority filtering is available with -p; for example, -p err narrows results to error-level messages. To programmatically consume logs, output JSON with -o json. You can also filter by a process ID with _PID=1234 to trace activity from a single process. A concrete example: to find recent ssh errors since this morning, combine unit, priority and time range. A common misconception is to rely solely on grepping text files; journalctl's native filters are more efficient and reduce false positives. Practice these commands until they become second nature for rapid incident triage. Essential journalctl Queries means use unit, priority, pid and time filters in journalctl instead of blindly grepping text logs.. content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.4 › Essential journalctl Queries
Common Commands
journalctl journalctl -f journalctl -u sshd journalctl -k journalctl -p err journalctl --since "2023-01-01 10:00:00" --until "2023-01-01 10:30:00" journalctl _PID=1234 journalctl -o json

Combine filters for precise queries and pipe to less or jq for further processing.

Example
Find sshd errors in the last 24 hours
journalctl -u sshd --since "24 hours ago" -p err

This returns only error-level entries for the sshd unit in the last day, reducing noise and speeding analysis.

Misconception

Using journalctl without filters returns huge output. Always scope queries with unit, priority, or time ranges for efficient triage.

screens.title: Make systemd Journal Persistent
screens.narratorSegment: By default journald may keep logs only in volatile memory under /run/log/journal, which are lost after a reboot. If your operations require durable history, make journald persistent. The process is straightforward: create the directory /var/log/journal with appropriate permissions and restart systemd-journald. This causes journald to write structured journal files under /var/log/journal so entries survive reboots. A concrete verification step is to list boots with the journalctl --list-boots command before and after a reboot to confirm older boots remain available. A common mistake is creating the directory but not restarting journald, or placing incorrect ownership and permissions so journald cannot write files. Use sudo mkdir -p /var/log/journal and then restart the service; verify with journalctl --list-boots and by checking file timestamps under /var/log/journal. Persisting the journal is valuable for forensic timelines and long-term troubleshooting, but remember persistent journals consume disk space and should be part of your retention policy. In practical terms, steps to retain journal across reboots. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.4 › Make systemd Journal Persistent
Steps
  1. Create the persistent directory: sudo mkdir -p /var/log/journal
  2. Restart journald: sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald
  3. Verify with journalctl --list-boots and inspect /var/log/journal for files.
sudo mkdir -p /var/log/journal sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald journalctl --list-boots

If files are present under /var/log/journal after restart, the journal is persistent. Monitor disk usage and rotate old journal files if necessary.

Pitfalls
  • Forgetting to restart journald after creating the directory.
  • Incorrect permissions preventing journald from writing files.
  • Not planning for disk usage of persistent journals.
Key Takeaway

Making the journal persistent preserves boot history for investigations, but requires disk planning and permissions checks.

screens.title: logrotate: Why and How
screens.narratorSegment: Log files grow over time and can consume all available disk space if not managed. logrotate automates rotation, compression, removal and mailing of logs on a schedule. It reads a main configuration file and per-service rules under /etc/logrotate. d/. A typical block specifies when to rotate, how many archived copies to keep, and whether to compress older files. For example, rotating daily and keeping seven copies balances recent access with disk limits. After rotation you often need the service to reopen its log file; logrotate supports postrotate scripts to reload or restart services. A common mistake is forgetting to set correct create permissions so the service cannot write to the newly created file. Another mistake is rotating too infrequently or keeping too many copies, which wastes space. The practical benefit is predictable disk usage and a simpler archive of past logs for audits and investigations. content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.4 › logrotate: Why and How
Purpose

Rotate and compress logs to prevent disk exhaustion and keep a manageable archive for audits.

Key directives
  • daily | weekly | monthly — rotation frequency
  • rotate N — keep N archived copies
  • compress / delaycompress — gzip compression behavior
  • create mode owner group — permissions for new file
Example
/var/log/nginx/*.log {
    daily
    missingok
    rotate 7
    compress
    delaycompress
    notifempty
    create 0640 nginx adm
    postrotate
        systemctl reload nginx.service > /dev/null 2>&1 || true
    endscript
}

This rotates Nginx logs daily, keeps 7 compressed copies, and reloads Nginx so it writes to the new log.

screens.title: Create a logrotate Rule for a Custom App
screens.narratorSegment: When you run a custom application that writes logs, add a logrotate rule so old files are compressed and removed automatically. Imagine your app writes to /var/log/myapp/access. log. Create a file under /etc/logrotate. d/myapp containing rotation directives: set daily rotation, keep three rotated copies, compress old files, and create a new file with correct permissions. After saving the file, test the configuration with logrotate in debug mode to see planned actions without making changes. Then force rotation to apply it immediately and inspect the directory to confirm access. log.1. gz exists. Verify with ls -l to find the compressed rotated file. A common trap is forgetting create with proper owner and mode; this can leave services unable to write to the new log and produce silent failures. screens.title: Basic Log Analysis with Shell Tools
screens.narratorSegment: Text-based logs are easily parsed with standard shell tools, which are invaluable for quick analysis. A common task is finding failed SSH logins in auth. log. Start by grepping for the phrase that indicates a failed attempt. Then extract the IP address with awk, sort the results, and use uniq -c to count occurrences. Finally sort numerically to surface the top offenders. This pipeline quickly identifies persistent sources of failed logins. For example, a one-line pipeline can show counts of unique IP addresses that have failed to authenticate. Another pattern is to search for repeated error messages across a service log and use timestamps to identify when the issue began. Beware common pitfalls: logs rotate, so check multiple rotated files or use the journal for structured queries. Also watch for inconsistent log formats; the field you extract with awk may appear in different positions if log entries vary. As a takeaway, develop short, reusable pipelines that answer specific operational questions rapidly. Module 08 › Chapter 8.4 › Basic Log Analysis
Quick Pipelines
# Find failed SSH attempts and count unique IPs sudo grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $11}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr # Count repeated error messages in a log sudo grep "error" /var/log/myapp/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr # Use journalctl for a service and filter by priority journalctl -u sshd -p err --since "24 hours ago"
Concrete example

The pipeline above prints counts and top IPs. Investigate top entries by performing a lookup or blocking when warranted.

Common pitfalls
  • Assuming field positions are fixed across all log lines.
  • Overlooking rotated or compressed logs; include older files when necessary.

screens.title: Operational Best Practices and Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: When managing logs in production, several recurring mistakes cause real operational pain. First, ignoring logs until an incident occurs leaves you without context when you need it most. Make daily or weekly checks part of routine operations. Second, failing to rotate logs or set retention can fill disks; configure logrotate with sensible frequency and retention that match log volume. Third, not making journald persistent leads to lost diagnostic data after reboots; create /var/log/journal when boot history is required. Fourth, leaving logs world-readable can expose sensitive data; set strict file permissions such as 0640 and limit access to administrators. Fifth, over-logging or under-logging both harm analysis; tune verbosity so it captures needed detail without overwhelming storage. Finally, test changes: after editing rsyslog or logrotate configs, restart services and validate the expected files and behavior. A short checklist helps prevent these issues: verify persistence, validate rotation, check permissions, and confirm forwarding. Ending question: which of these mistakes is most likely on your systems and how will you fix it? fullNarratorScript:
System logs are the primary evidence of what happened on a Linux server. They record user logins, service starts and stops, kernel messages, and application output. In practice, logs power troubleshooting, performance investigations, and security detection. If you can read, filter, and rotate logs reliably, you can find the root cause of many incidents and preserve evidence when something goes wrong. In this chapter we focus on two complementary stacks: traditional syslog daemons such as rsyslog for collecting and forwarding text logs, and the systemd journal managed by journald for structured, queryable logs. We also cover tools you will use every day: journalctl for targeted queries and logrotate to keep files from growing indefinitely. You will learn concrete configuration examples, how to make the journal persistent across reboots, and how to write a logrotate policy for a custom application. By the end you will be able to inspect service logs, centralize logs if needed, rotate and compress old files, and run basic analyses to find failed logins or repeated errors. Consider which log file on your system you would protect first and why.

In this chapter you will gain practical skills that are immediately useful on a Linux server. First, you'll learn why logs are essential for security, troubleshooting and compliance, and how to find the right log for a specific problem. Second, you'll configure rsyslog so it collects and forwards messages based on facility and priority, and you'll practice sending logs to a central collector. Third, you'll use journalctl to query systemd journal entries by service, priority, PID and time range, and make the journal persistent across reboots. Fourth, you'll implement logrotate policies to automate rotation, compression and retention for application logs. Each objective focuses on applied tasks: editing configuration files, running commands to verify behavior, and using small search and aggregation pipelines to extract meaning from noisy logs. As you progress, verify ownership and permissions for log files and test rotation or forwarding in a safe environment. These skills ensure you can keep logs reliable, manageable, and useful when incidents occur.

These applied objectives focus on short hands-on steps you can perform and test. You will make the systemd journal persistent so logs survive a reboot and verify with a boot list. You will create a logrotate policy for a dummy application, run logrotate in debug and force modes, and inspect the rotated and compressed files. You will configure a minimal rsyslog forwarding rule to send all messages to a remote collector, and test that the collector receives messages. Finally, you will practice simple analysis: find failed SSH logins and count unique IP addresses. Each task has a clear verification: a persistent journal directory, rotated files with. gz suffixes, a working rsyslog client that forwards messages, and a short grep/awk pipeline that counts offending IPs. These verification steps make the learning concrete and repeatable for operational work.

System logs are chronological records of events produced by the kernel, init systems, services and applications. They capture state changes such as user authentication events, service start and stop events, kernel warnings, and application errors. Logs are essential because they provide an audit trail for troubleshooting and security investigations. For example, when a service crashes, log entries around the crash time reveal the preceding actions and error messages. A concrete scenario: a sudden spike in failed SSH authentication entries in auth. log indicates either a misconfiguration or a brute force attempt. Without logs you cannot determine the origin or timeline. A common misconception is that logging is passive and low priority; in reality, logs must be intentionally configured, rotated, and protected. If logs are world-readable or not rotated, you risk exposure or disk exhaustion. Key operational concerns include choosing which events to log, ensuring timestamps are consistent, and securing log files with correct permissions. As a takeaway, treat logs as critical telemetry: decide what to preserve, where to store it, and how long to keep it so you can answer who did what and when.

rsyslog is a traditional syslog daemon used widely to collect and forward text-based system messages. Two core concepts drive rsyslog rules: facility and priority. A facility indicates the source or category of a message — examples include auth, mail, cron, and kernel. Priority indicates severity levels like info, warning, error, crit and emerg. In configuration files you combine facility and priority to decide where messages go. For instance, the rule authpriv.* /var/log/auth. log records all authentication-related messages in a dedicated file. Another common rule, *. info;mail. none;authpriv. none;cron. none /var/log/messages, writes all informational messages except those from mail, authpriv, and cron to a general file. Practically, group sensitive logs like authentication into separate files so access controls can be stricter. A frequent mistake is mis-ordering rules or forgetting to escape characters; always validate syntax and restart the rsyslog service after changes. As a takeaway, use facility and priority intentionally to separate sensitive messages and simplify later analysis. rsyslog Basics: Facility and Priority means use facility and priority selectors to direct messages to the right files and destinations for clarity and security.. In practical terms, how rsyslog classifies and routes messages. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Centralizing logs to a dedicated collector simplifies monitoring and preserves logs if an individual host is compromised. To configure a collector, enable the appropriate input modules in rsyslog. For UDP, uncomment module(load="imudp") and enable input(type="imudp" port="514"). For TCP you can enable imtcp similarly. On clients, add a forwarding rule such as *.* @logserver_ip:514 to send messages via UDP or *.* @@logserver_ip:514 for TCP. Always secure the transport where possible, for example by using TLS or a private network. After editing configuration files on both sides, restart rsyslog on collector and clients. A common operational step is to apply filters on the collector to place incoming messages into host-specific directories or to tag them for easier indexing. Misconfiguration risks include port conflicts, firewall blocking, or unintentional flooding of the network with logs. As a practical check, generate a test message with logger and confirm it appears on the collector. This ensures forwarding and reception are working end-to-end. Configuring rsyslog for Centralization means forward logs to a dedicated, secured collector to simplify analysis and protect evidence from compromised hosts.. In practical terms, enable receiving on a collector and forward from clients. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

systemd's journald collects logs from multiple sources — the kernel, initrd, services and applications that write to standard output or standard error. Unlike plain text files, journald stores logs in a structured binary journal which enables powerful querying. journalctl is the command-line tool that reads this journal and provides rich filters. Unlike tailing text files, you can filter by unit name, priority, process ID, time range, and output format such as JSON for programmatic parsing. A common confusion is to think journald replaces rsyslog; they serve complementary roles. You can forward journal entries to a syslog daemon or have rsyslog collect text files, so use both where appropriate. Another important operational note: by default journald stores logs in volatile memory under /run/log/journal, which is lost on reboot. If you need persistent logs, create /var/log/journal and restart systemd-journald. In short, journald offers fast, structured querying while rsyslog excels at stable, text-based forwarding and long-term storage. journald and journalctl means use journalctl for fast, precise queries and make journald persistent when you need durable logs across reboots.. In practical terms, how systemd's journal stores and exposes logs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

journalctl offers concise filters that save time when you search for evidence. Start with the basics: journalctl shows the full journal while journalctl -f follows new entries in real time. To view logs for a single service, use journalctl -u followed by the unit name; for example, filtering sshd quickly surfaces authentication-related messages from that daemon. To inspect kernel messages only, use journalctl -k. You can limit results by time range with --since and --until for targeted investigations. Priority filtering is available with -p; for example, -p err narrows results to error-level messages. To programmatically consume logs, output JSON with -o json. You can also filter by a process ID with _PID=1234 to trace activity from a single process. A concrete example: to find recent ssh errors since this morning, combine unit, priority and time range. A common misconception is to rely solely on grepping text files; journalctl's native filters are more efficient and reduce false positives. Practice these commands until they become second nature for rapid incident triage. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

By default journald may keep logs only in volatile memory under /run/log/journal, which are lost after a reboot. If your operations require durable history, make journald persistent. The process is straightforward: create the directory /var/log/journal with appropriate permissions and restart systemd-journald. This causes journald to write structured journal files under /var/log/journal so entries survive reboots. A concrete verification step is to list boots with the journalctl --list-boots command before and after a reboot to confirm older boots remain available. A common mistake is creating the directory but not restarting journald, or placing incorrect ownership and permissions so journald cannot write files. Use sudo mkdir -p /var/log/journal and then restart the service; verify with journalctl --list-boots and by checking file timestamps under /var/log/journal. Persisting the journal is valuable for forensic timelines and long-term troubleshooting, but remember persistent journals consume disk space and should be part of your retention policy. Make systemd Journal Persistent means create /var/log/journal and restart systemd-journald so historical boot logs are retained for analysis.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Log files grow over time and can consume all available disk space if not managed. logrotate automates rotation, compression, removal and mailing of logs on a schedule. It reads a main configuration file and per-service rules under /etc/logrotate. d/. A typical block specifies when to rotate, how many archived copies to keep, and whether to compress older files. For example, rotating daily and keeping seven copies balances recent access with disk limits. After rotation you often need the service to reopen its log file; logrotate supports postrotate scripts to reload or restart services. A common mistake is forgetting to set correct create permissions so the service cannot write to the newly created file. When managing logs in production, several recurring mistakes cause real operational pain. First, ignoring logs until an incident occurs leaves you without context when you need it most.
